questions.question:
Consider the following data path diagram.

Consider an instruction: [latex]R0\leftarrow R1+R2[/latex]. The following steps are used to execute it over the given data path. Assume that PC is incremented appropriately. The subscripts r and w indicate read and write operations, respectively.

[latex]1. \; R2_r,TEMP1_r,ALU_{add},TEMP2_w[/latex]
[latex]2. \; R1_r,TEMP1_w[/latex]
[latex]3. \; PC_r,MAR_w,MEM_r[/latex]
[latex]4. \; TEMP2_r,R0_w[/latex]
[latex]5. \; MDR_r,IR_w[/latex]

Which one of the following is the correct order of execution of the above steps?
questions.explanation:
First fetch the instruction, then execute it:
- 3: PC [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] MAR, read memory (fetch)
- 5: MDR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] IR (instruction now in IR)
- 2: R1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TEMP1 (one ALU input is latched in TEMP1)
- 1: R2 on the bus + TEMP1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] ALU add [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] TEMP2
- 4: TEMP2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R0

Answer: 3, 5, 2, 1, 4

questions.question: Which one of the following facilitates transfer of bulk data from hard disk to main memory with the highest throughput?
questions.explanation:
In DMA, the DMA controller moves the whole block between disk and memory directly, without the CPU handling every word. Interrupt-driven, polling and programmed I/O all need the CPU for each word, so they are much slower for bulk data.

questions.question: A 32-bit wide main memory unit with a capacity of 1 GB is built using 256M x 4-bit DRAM chips. The number of rows of memory cells in the DRAM chip is [latex]2^{14}[/latex]. The time taken to perform one refresh operation is 50 nanoseconds. The refresh period is 2 milliseconds. The percentage (rounded to the closest integer) of the time available for performing the memory read/write operations in the main memory unit is __________.

Each 256M [latex]\times[/latex] 4 chip refreshes its [latex]2^{14}[/latex] rows one at a time: [latex]2^{14}\times50[/latex] ns = 819.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s in every 2 ms (all chips refresh in parallel).

Refresh takes 0.8192 / 2 = 40.96% of the time, leaving about 59% for reads and writes.

Answer: 59

questions.question: A direct mapped cache memory of 1 MB has a block size of 256 bytes. The cache has an access time of 3 ns and a hit rate of 94%. During a cache miss, it takes 20 ns to bring the first word of a block from the main memory, while each subsequent word takes 5 ns. The word size is 64 bits. The average memory access time in ns (round off to 1 decimal place) is______.
questions.explanation:
Block = 256 bytes = 32 words of 8 bytes.
Miss penalty = first word 20 ns + 31 more words [latex]\times[/latex] 5 ns = 175 ns.

Average access time = hit time + miss rate [latex]\times[/latex] miss penalty = [latex]3+0.06\times175=3+10.5=13.5[/latex] ns.

(If cache access is counted only on hits: [latex]0.94\times3+0.06\times175\approx13.3[/latex], which the official key also accepts.)

Answer: 13.5

Other Answer as per GATE 2020 Answer Key : 13.3 to 13.3 or 13.5 to 13.5

questions.question:
A non-pipelined instruction execution unit operating at 2 GHz takes an average of
6 cycles to execute an instruction of a program P. The unit is then redesigned to
operate on a 5-stage pipeline at 2 GHz. Assume that the ideal throughput of the
pipelined unit is 1 instruction per cycle. In the execution of program P,
20% instructions incur an average of 2 cycles stall due to data hazards and
20% instructions incur an average of 3 cycles stall due to control hazards. The
speedup (rounded off to one decimal place) obtained by the pipelined design over
the non-pipelined design is ________
questions.explanation:
Non-pipelined: 6 cycles per instruction.
Pipelined CPI [latex]=1+0.2\times2+0.2\times3=1+0.4+0.6=2[/latex]

Same clock (2 GHz), so speedup [latex]=6/2=3.0[/latex]

Answer: 3

questions.question:
A given program has 25% load/store instructions. Suppose the ideal CPI (cycles per
instruction) without any memory stalls is 2. The program exhibits 2% miss rate on
instruction cache and 8% miss rate on data cache. The miss penalty is 100 cycles.
The speedup (rounded off to two decimal places) achieved with a perfect cache (i.e.,
with NO data or instruction cache misses) is _________
questions.explanation:
Every instruction is fetched (I-cache) and 25% also access data (D-cache).

Stall cycles per instruction:
- I-cache: [latex]1\times0.02\times100=2[/latex]
- D-cache: [latex]0.25\times0.08\times100=2[/latex]

Actual CPI [latex]=2+2+2=6[/latex], perfect-cache CPI [latex]=2[/latex].

Speedup [latex]=6/2=3.00[/latex]

Answer: 3

questions.question: A 5-stage pipelined processor has Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Write Operand (WO) stages. The IF, ID, OF and WO stages take 1 clock cycle each for any instruction. The PO stage takes 1 clock cycle for ADD and SUB instructions, 3 clock cycles for MUL instruction, and 6 clock cycles for DIV instruction respectively. Operand forwarding is used in the pipeline. What is the number of clock cycles needed to execute the following sequence of instructions?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- I0 MUL: IF 1, ID 2, OF 3, PO 4-6, WO 7
- I1 DIV: IF 2, ID 3, OF 4, PO 7-12, WO 13
- I2 ADD (needs R5 from DIV, forwarded): PO 13, WO 14
- I3 SUB (needs R2 from ADD, forwarded): PO 14, WO 15

Answer: 15

questions.question:
A processor with 16 general purpose registers uses a 32-bit instruction format. The
instruction format consists of an opcode field, an addressing mode field, two register
operand fields, and a 16-bit scalar field. If 8 addressing modes are to be supported,
the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for every addressing mode
is _________
questions.explanation:
Divide the 32 bits among the fields:
- 16 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 bits per register field, two fields = 8 bits
- 8 addressing modes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 3 bits
- Scalar field = 16 bits

Opcode bits [latex]=32-8-3-16=5[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]2^5=32[/latex] opcodes.

Answer: 32

questions.question:
Consider a hard disk with a rotational speed of [latex]15000[/latex] rpm. The time to move the read/write head from a track to its adjacent track is [latex]1[/latex] millisecond. Initially, the head is on track [latex]0[/latex]. The number of sectors per track is [latex]400[/latex]. The sector size is [latex]1024[/latex] bytes. It is necessary to transfer data from [latex]10[/latex] randomly located sectors in each of the following tracks in the order: [latex]5, 12[/latex] and [latex]7[/latex].

The total time for the data transfer (in milliseconds) from the hard disk is ________. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Rotation time per revolution [latex]=\dfrac{60000\text{ ms}}{15000}=4[/latex] ms, so average rotational latency (half a revolution) [latex]=2[/latex] ms, and time per sector [latex]=\dfrac{4\text{ ms}}{400\text{ sectors}}=0.01[/latex] ms.

Seek time (head moves [latex]1[/latex] ms per adjacent track, following the path [latex]0\to5\to12\to7[/latex]):
[latex]0\to5[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms; [latex]5\to12[/latex]: [latex]7[/latex] tracks [latex]=7[/latex] ms; [latex]12\to7[/latex]: [latex]5[/latex] tracks [latex]=5[/latex] ms. Total seek [latex]=5+7+5=17[/latex] ms.

Data transfer per track: since the [latex]10[/latex] sectors needed are randomly located, each individual sector access requires (on average) a fresh rotational latency of [latex]2[/latex] ms before the required sector arrives under the head, plus the [latex]0.01[/latex] ms to actually read it:
Per track [latex]=10\times(2+0.01)=20.1[/latex] ms. Over [latex]3[/latex] tracks: [latex]3\times20.1=60.3[/latex] ms.

Total time [latex]=[/latex] seek [latex]+[/latex] transfer [latex]=17+60.3=77.3[/latex] ms.

Answer: 77.3

questions.question:
Instructions execution in a processor is divided into 5 stages. Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID) , Operand Fetch (OF), Execute (EX), and Write Back (WB), These stages take 5,4,20, 10 and 3 nanoseconds (ns) respectively. A pipelined implementation of the processor requires buffering between each pair of consecutive stages with a delay of 2ns.
Two pipelined implementations of the processor are contemplated.

(i) a naive pipeline implementation (NP) with 5 stages and
(ii) an efficient pipeline (EP) where the OF stage id divided into stages OF1 and OF2 with execution times of 12 ns and 8 ns respectively.

The speedup (correct to two decimals places) achieved by EP over NP in executing 20 independent instructions with no hazards is ________________.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- NP: slowest stage 20 + 2 (buffer) = 22 ns; 5 stages, 20 instructions [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (5 + 19) [latex]\times[/latex] 22 = 528 ns
- EP: stages 5, 4, 12, 8, 10, 3 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] slowest 12 + 2 = 14 ns; (6 + 19) [latex]\times[/latex] 14 = 350 ns

Speedup = 528 / 350 [latex]\approx[/latex] 1.51

Answer: 1.51

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.question: Consider a processor with 64 registers  and an instruction set of size twelve. Each instruction has five distinct fields, namely, opcode, two source register identifiers, one destination register identifier, and a twelve-bit immediate value. Each instruction must be stored in memory in  byte-aligned fashion. If a program has 100 instructions, the amount of memory(in bytes) consumed by the program text is _____ .
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Opcode: 12 instructions [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 4 bits
- 3 register fields: 64 registers [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 6 bits each = 18 bits
- Immediate: 12 bits

Total = 34 bits [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] byte-aligned = 5 bytes per instruction. 100 instructions [latex]\times[/latex] 5 = 500 bytes.

Answer: 500

questions.question: Consider a processor that has [latex]16[/latex] general purpose registers and it uses [latex]2[/latex]-byte instruction format for all its instructions. Variable-sized opcodes are permitted. There are three different types of instructions; M-type, R-type, and C-type. Each M-type instruction has [latex]2[/latex] register operands and a [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate operand. Each Rtype instruction has [latex]3[/latex] register operands. Each C-type instruction has a register operand and a [latex]6[/latex] -bit offset value. If there are [latex]2[/latex] unique M-type opcodes and [latex]7[/latex] unique R-type opcodes, which one of the following options gives the maximum number of unique opcodes possible for C-type instructions?
questions.explanation:
With [latex]16[/latex] general-purpose registers, each register operand needs [latex]\log_2 16=4[/latex] bits. The full instruction is [latex]2[/latex] bytes [latex]=16[/latex] bits.

- M-type: [latex]2[/latex] register operands ([latex]8[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit immediate [latex]=14[/latex] bits of operand, leaving [latex]16-14=2[/latex] bits for the opcode → up to [latex]2^2=4[/latex] possible M-type codes, but only [latex]2[/latex] are actually used, leaving [latex]4-2=2[/latex] unused [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes free for other instruction types.
- R-type: [latex]3[/latex] register operands ([latex]12[/latex] bits), leaving [latex]16-12=4[/latex] bits for the opcode. Using an "expanding opcode" scheme, the [latex]2[/latex] leftover [latex]2[/latex]-bit prefixes (not used by M-type) each expand into [latex]2^{4-2}=4[/latex] possible [latex]4[/latex]-bit codes, giving [latex]2\times4=8[/latex] total available R-type slots; only [latex]7[/latex] are used, leaving [latex]8-7=1[/latex] unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix.
- C-type: [latex]1[/latex] register operand ([latex]4[/latex] bits) [latex]+[/latex] [latex]6[/latex]-bit offset [latex]=10[/latex] bits, leaving [latex]16-10=6[/latex] bits for the opcode. That single unused [latex]4[/latex]-bit prefix expands into [latex]2^{6-4}=4[/latex] possible [latex]6[/latex]-bit C-type codes.

Answer: 4

questions.question:
The baseline execution time of a program on a 2 GHz single core machine is 100 nanoseconds (ns). The code corresponding to 90% of the execution time can be fully parallelized. The overhead for using an additional core is 10 ns when running on a multicore system. Assume that all cores in the multicore system run their share of the parallelized code for an equal amount of time.
The number of cores that minimize the execution time of the program is _______
questions.explanation:
Serial part [latex]=10\%[/latex] of 100 ns = 10 ns, parallel part = 90 ns.
With [latex]p[/latex] cores: [latex]T(p)=10+\dfrac{90}{p}+10(p-1)[/latex]

- [latex]p=1[/latex]: 100 ns
- [latex]p=2[/latex]: [latex]10+45+10=65[/latex] ns
- [latex]p=3[/latex]: [latex]10+30+20=60[/latex] ns
- [latex]p=4[/latex]: [latex]10+22.5+30=62.5[/latex] ns

Minimum at [latex]p=3[/latex] (also from [latex]\frac{90}{p}=10p[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]p=3[/latex]).

Answer: 3

questions.question: Consider a memory system with 1M bytes of main memory and 16K bytes of cache memory. Assume that the processor generates 20-bit memory address, and the cache block size is 16 bytes. If the cache uses direct mapping, how many bits will be required to store all the tag values? [Assume memory is byte addressable, 1K = [latex]2^{10}[/latex], 1M = [latex]2^{20}[/latex].]
questions.explanation:
Cache [latex]=16\text{K}=2^{14}[/latex] bytes, block size [latex]=16=2^4[/latex] bytes, so number of cache lines [latex]=\dfrac{2^{14}}{2^4}=2^{10}[/latex] — index field [latex]=10[/latex] bits, offset field [latex]=4[/latex] bits.

Main memory [latex]=1\text{M}=2^{20}[/latex] bytes, byte-addressable, so the address is [latex]20[/latex] bits wide. Tag field [latex]=20-10-4=6[/latex] bits per line.

Total bits needed to store all tag values [latex]=6\text{ bits}\times2^{10}\text{ lines}=6\times2^{10}[/latex].

Answer: 6×2^10
